newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma blast kin want closed circuit TV expanded.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma blast kin want closed circuit TV expanded.

text.p: The families of victims of the Oklahoma City bombing on Monday urged the trial judge in the case to set up a closed-circuit telecast of all court proceedings, not just the trial.

Since the trial for the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building has been moved to Denver, victims and relatives of those killed have complained that Judge Richard Matsch has disregarded their feelings.
The victims said they also want Matsch to designate a large facility -- perhaps an Air Force base in suburban Oklahoma City -- for the telecast, rather than a smaller courtroom that he has chosen.
Timothy McVeigh and former Army buddy Terry Nichols have been charged in the blast. They will be tried separately with McVeigh going first, on March 31. The two face the death penalty if convicted.

A U.S. anti-terrorism law contains a provision requiring a closed-circuit telecast of the "criminal trial proceedings" of the case to spare victims the hardship of travelling to Denver. The case was moved from Oklahoma to ensure a fairer hearing.

The victims argue that that word "proceedings" includes pre-trial hearings. Some victims and relatives of those killed in the bombing have travelled to Denver for pre-trial hearings, but some have said the trip was difficult, despite offers of free lodging and travel subsidies.

Although prosecutors have identified more than 2,000 victims, Matsch has chosen a courtroom in Oklahoma City for the closed-circuit telecast that seats about 150 people. The victims suggested nearby Tinker Air Force Base as an ideal site for the closed-circuit telecast.

They also want Matsch to let them participate in how the technology for the telecast is chosen. Matsch has said he wants to make sure the broadcast signal is not pirated because the law intends the telecast only to be viewed by the victims.
The group asked the judge to hold a hearing on the matter by Jan. 10 and said if he does not, they "intend to seek extraordinary relief" from an appeals court.
The blast at the federal building killed 168 people.
